Case Title: Satya v. Teja Singh
Acts Cited: Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Hindu Marriage Act 1955
Sections Cited: Section 488 CrPC (1898), Section 125 CrPC (1973), Section 144 BNSS (2023), Section 13 CPC
Legal Topics: Foreign Divorce Decree Validity, Private International Law, Fraud on Jurisdiction, Maintenance of Abandoned Spouse
Outcome: Appeal Allowed; Ex-parte Nevada decree declared null and void in India; Maintenance restored in favor of wife under Indian law.
Fact/Petitioner: Wife married respondent in Punjab according to Hindu rites in 1955. Respondent moved to USA in 1959 for higher studies and secured employment, abandoning wife and two infant children in India without providing maintenance.
Fact/Respondent: Husband went to Nevada, USA, stayed for a brief statutory residency period of 6 weeks purely to invoke the jurisdiction of the Second Judicial District Court of Nevada, obtaining an ex-parte divorce decree on December 30, 1964.
Issues: Whether a foreign ex-parte decree of divorce obtained in Nevada through fraudulent representation of domicile can dissolve a Hindu marriage solemnized in India and extinguish the wife's right to maintenance under Section 488 CrPC (now Section 125 CrPC / Section 144 BNSS)?
Petitioner Argument: The Nevada court had no true personal or territorial jurisdiction. The husband was never permanently domiciled in Nevada; the foreign decree was procured through fraud on jurisdictional facts and cannot be recognized under Section 13 CPC.
Respondent Argument: The marriage was validly dissolved by a competent foreign court in Nevada where the husband resided; consequently, the applicant ceased to be his wife and is disqualified from claiming maintenance under Indian criminal procedure.
Factors to be Considered: Distinction between bona fide domicile and transient residency; public policy of protecting abandoned Indian spouses; doctrine that English common law rule of wife's domicile merging into husband's does not apply to perpetuate fraud; Section 13(e) CPC (judgment obtained by fraud).
Decision: Nevada divorce was a nullity in Indian law because the husband lacked genuine domicile and practiced fraud upon the foreign court. The marital tie subsists and the husband remains legally bound to pay maintenance to his wife and children under Indian law.
Exact Holding: True holding: Supreme Court struck down Nevada divorce decree obtained after 6 weeks stay and restored wife's maintenance under Section 488 CrPC (1898), holding that a foreign judgment obtained by fraud on jurisdiction is unenforceable under Section 13(e) CPC.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT establish that all foreign divorces are automatically invalid in India. If a foreign court has genuine jurisdiction, applies the proper personal law, or the respondent voluntarily submits and contests on the merits, the decree may be recognized under Section 13 CPC.
Calculator Dependency: Private International Law Section 13 CPC Foreign Divorce recognition checklist.

Case Title: Y. Narasimha Rao & Ors. v. Y. Venkata Lakshmi & Anr.
Acts Cited: Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Hindu Marriage Act 1955, Indian Penal Code 1860
Sections Cited: Section 13 CPC, Section 494 IPC, Section 11 HMA
Legal Topics: Foreign Matrimonial Decrees, Private International Law, Section 13 CPC Rules, Bigamy Prosecution
Outcome: Appeal Dismissed; Missouri divorce decree declared null and void in India; prosecution of husband under Section 494 IPC for bigamy upheld.
Fact/Petitioner: Wife married respondent in Tirupati according to Hindu Vedic rites in 1975. Husband left for the United States, obtained employment, and subsequently filed for divorce in the Circuit Court of St. Louis County, Missouri, alleging irretrievable breakdown of marriage.
Fact/Respondent: Husband filed a petition in Missouri stating 90 days residency. Wife sent a reply under protest from India stating she did not submit to Missouri jurisdiction. Husband obtained decree and remarried.
Issues: What are the binding rules under Section 13 CPC for recognizing or refusing to recognize foreign matrimonial judgments dissolving marriages solemnized in India under Hindu law?
Petitioner Argument: Marriage solemnized under Hindu Marriage Act cannot be dissolved by a foreign court applying foreign grounds (such as irretrievable breakdown) not recognized under the Hindu Marriage Act. Foreign decree is opposed to Section 13(a), (b), (c) and (d) CPC.
Respondent Argument: Missouri court was competent under its local law, and wife was served with process; foreign dissolution of marriage is valid internationally.
Factors to be Considered: Harmonious construction of Section 13(a) to 13(f) CPC; rule that marriage must be dissolved under the law under which parties married; requirement that respondent voluntarily and unconditionally submits to jurisdiction without protest; requirement of decision on actual merits.
Decision: Supreme Court laid down three definitive rules: (1) Foreign court must have jurisdiction recognized by Indian private international law; (2) Marriage can only be dissolved under matrimonial law governing the parties; (3) Respondent must voluntarily submit without protest.
Exact Holding: True holding: 2-judge bench ruled that a foreign divorce decree passed on grounds unknown to the personal law of the parties (such as irretrievable breakdown of marriage under Missouri law) without voluntary submission by the non-resident spouse is void under Section 13 CPC.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT bar foreign divorces where the foreign court applies Indian personal law, or where both parties are genuinely domiciled abroad and contest on grounds recognized by Indian statutes, or where the respondent voluntarily and unconditionally submits.
Calculator Dependency: Private International Law foreign decree adjudication engine.

Case Title: Rajnesh v. Neha & Anr.
Judges: Indu Malhotra, R. Subhash Reddy, JJ.
Acts Cited: Code of Criminal Procedure 1973, Hindu Marriage Act 1955, Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act 1956, Special Marriage Act 1954
Sections Cited: Section 125 CrPC, Section 144 BNSS, Section 24 HMA, Section 12 DV Act, Section 20 DV Act, Section 18 HAMA
Legal Topics: Uniform Maintenance Guidelines, Mandatory Affidavit of Assets and Liabilities, Overlapping Maintenance Remedies, Maintenance from Date of Application
Outcome: Appeal Disposed; Comprehensive nationwide binding guidelines framed; Mandatory disclosure of comprehensive income/assets affidavits enforced.
Fact/Petitioner: Wife left matrimonial home with minor son due to persistent domestic friction and cruelty. She filed for interim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC. Family Court awarded maintenance which husband contested on grounds of financial incapacity.
Fact/Respondent: Husband claimed business failure, heavy liabilities, and argued that wife had independent earning capacity.
Issues: How to resolve overlapping maintenance jurisdictions, determine quantum uniformly, eliminate delays, and enforce disclosure of authentic financial status?
Petitioner Argument: Husband lives an affluent lifestyle, holds undisclosed commercial assets, and purposefully conceals his income to starve the wife and minor child into submission.
Respondent Argument: Maintenance orders passed under multiple overlapping enactments (CrPC, HMA, DV Act) lead to conflicting claims and unjust enrichment.
Factors to be Considered: Status of parties; reasonable needs of wife and children; independent income and property of claimant; husband's lifestyle and actual earning capacity; standard of living during cohabitation; inflation and education expenses.
Decision: Supreme Court instituted mandatory Affidavit of Disclosure of Assets and Liabilities across all courts; held maintenance must be awarded from date of application; ordered adjustment of overlapping awards.
Exact Holding: True holding: Supreme Court formulated comprehensive nationwide guidelines directing that maintenance in all proceedings shall date back to the date of application, requiring comprehensive sworn disclosure of assets and liabilities, and mandating set-off of overlapping awards.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT prescribe fixed numerical percentages of income for maintenance; explicitly directs trial courts to exercise judicial discretion based on the exhaustive checklist of factors.
Calculator Dependency: Quantum evaluation framework, overlapping maintenance adjustment, retrospective interest from application date.

Case Title: Kalyan Dey Chowdhury v. Rita Dey Chowdhury Nee Nandy
Judges: R. Banumathi, Mohan M. Shantanagoudar, JJ.
Acts Cited: Hindu Marriage Act 1955
Legal Topics: Permanent Alimony, Quantum of Maintenance, 25% Net Salary Indicative Benchmark, Disposable Income
Outcome: Appeal Disposed; Permanent maintenance fixed at Rs. 20,000 per month (~25% of husband's net monthly income).
Fact/Petitioner: Husband challenged High Court order enhancing maintenance for divorced wife to Rs 23,000 per month, contending it exceeded his financial capacity.
Fact/Respondent: Divorced wife sought adequate permanent alimony commensurate with the husband's net salary and comfortable social standing.
Issues: What is the appropriate benchmark percentage of husband's net disposable salary that should be awarded as permanent alimony/maintenance to the wife?
Petitioner Argument: High Court committed an error in enhancing maintenance without properly verifying the net take-home salary after compulsory deductions.
Respondent Argument: Wife is entitled to live with dignity and in a manner commensurate with the status and income enjoyed by the husband.
Factors to be Considered: Principles in Dr. Kulbhushan Kumar v. Raj Kumari (1970) 3 SCC 129; 25% of net salary of the husband as a just and proper benchmark; deductions for taxes and statutory contributions.
Decision: Following Dr. Kulbhushan Kumar, Supreme Court held that 25% of the husband's net salary was just and proper maintenance for the wife in the facts of the case.
Exact Holding: True holding: Following Dr. Kulbhushan Kumar v. Raj Kumari (1970) 3 SCC 129, Supreme Court awarded 25% of the husband's net disposable income as permanent maintenance under Section 25 HMA.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT establish an absolute, rigid statutory cap or entitlement of 25%. It is an indicative judicial guideline on the facts of that case. Maintenance can vary higher or lower depending on children's needs, independent income, and health conditions.
Calculator Dependency: Configurable spousal maintenance guideline (default 25%, adjustable by user/advocate between 15% and 35%).

Case Title: Dr. Kulbhushan Kumar v. Raj Kumari & Anr.
Judges: J.C. Shah, K.S. Hegde, A.N. Grover, JJ.
Acts Cited: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act 1956
Legal Topics: Maintenance Quantum, Net Income Calculation, One-Fourth Net Income Guideline
Outcome: Appeal Disposed; Maintenance fixed at 25% of husband's net income after deducting income tax.
Fact/Petitioner: Husband, a medical practitioner in government service, contested maintenance decree passed in favor of wife and minor daughter.
Fact/Respondent: Wife claimed maintenance commensurate with husband's position, asserting she was forced out of matrimonial home.
Issues: What deductions are permissible from husband's gross salary before computing maintenance percentage, and what is a reasonable proportion for the wife?
Petitioner Argument: Gross income cannot be the basis; compulsory tax, GPF, and professional expenses must be deducted before arriving at disposable income.
Respondent Argument: Voluntary deductions or loan repayments cannot be used to artificially depress maintenance.
Factors to be Considered: Only statutory compulsory deductions (income tax) can be subtracted from gross income; voluntary deductions like LIC premiums or savings cannot be deducted; one-fourth (25%) of net income represents a fair standard.
Decision: Supreme Court established the foundational rule that maintenance should be computed on net disposable income (gross minus compulsory taxes) and fixed 25% as the appropriate benchmark.
Exact Holding: True holding: 3-judge bench established that net income is arrived at after deducting compulsory statutory taxes, and that one-fourth (25%) of such net income is a just proportion for maintenance under Section 18 HAMA.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT establish a statutory ceiling; does not allow voluntary savings, luxury EMI repayments, or artificial deductions to be subtracted before computing maintenance.
Calculator Dependency: Net disposable income computation methodology (gross minus compulsory taxes).

Case Title: Devika Jain v. Rajesh Jain
Acts Cited: Hindu Marriage Act 1955
Legal Topics: NRI Maintenance, Purchasing Power Parity (PPP), Foreign Cost of Living Deductions, UK Earnings
Outcome: Appeal Disposed; Interim maintenance calibrated to reflect high foreign taxes and real living expenses in London, UK.
Fact/Petitioner: Wife claimed interim maintenance of Rs 1,50,000 per month based on husband's annual UK earnings of GBP 40,000.
Fact/Respondent: Husband demonstrated that after deducting UK income tax, National Insurance, London accommodation rent, council tax, and transport, his actual disposable income was modest.
Issues: Whether the gross salary earned by an NRI in foreign currency can be converted at spot exchange rates into INR to assess Indian maintenance without deducting local foreign taxes and living expenses?
Petitioner Argument: Husband earns a high salary in British Pounds; converting his gross salary to INR proves he has vast financial capacity.
Respondent Argument: Direct conversion of foreign currency without factoring in local cost of living and purchasing power parity creates an artificial and grossly unfair picture of wealth.
Factors to be Considered: Purchasing power parity; high tax rates in UK; mandatory local living expenses, council taxes, and accommodation costs in foreign jurisdictions.
Decision: Delhi High Court ruled that courts must evaluate the cost of living and tax structure of the country where the NRI resides; gross foreign salary cannot be converted directly without deducting local host-country expenditures.
Exact Holding: True holding: Division Bench held that in assessing maintenance against an overseas resident, courts must consider purchasing power parity and actual living expenses and taxes in the foreign country.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT create a fixed statutory 50% deduction. The deduction must be established through evidence of actual taxes, rent, and compulsory living expenses in the host country.
Calculator Dependency: Configurable foreign living-cost deduction parameter (user/advocate adjustable).

Case Title: Shikha v. Avaneesh Mahodaya
Acts Cited: Code of Criminal Procedure 1973
Legal Topics: NRI Software Engineer, US Dollar Salary, Foreign Living Expense Deductions, Section 125 CrPC Quantum
Outcome: Criminal Revision Disposed; Maintenance calibrated after accounting for high US living expenditures and mandatory taxes.
Fact/Petitioner: Wife residing in Indore filed for maintenance against husband who is a software engineer employed in the United States earning over USD 100,000 annually.
Fact/Respondent: Husband submitted pay stubs and Form 1040 demonstrating federal/state taxes, high apartment rent, health insurance, and car loan payments in the USA.
Issues: What proportion of US dollar salary should be awarded to the wife in India after accounting for host-country living expenses?
Petitioner Argument: Husband is earning millions of rupees when converted from USD; wife is entitled to standard of living matching his tech-salary status.
Respondent Argument: High nominal salary in USA is offset by heavy living costs, housing rent, medical insurance, and mandatory deductions.
Factors to be Considered: High expenditure required to maintain residence in the United States; local tax liabilities; standard of living of both parties; reasonable needs of the wife in Indore.
Decision: High Court confirmed that while NRI husband is obligated to pay substantial maintenance, the court must deduct mandatory host-country living expenses and taxes to arrive at true disposable income.
Exact Holding: True holding: High Court held that mandatory foreign living expenses and statutory taxes must be deducted from US dollar earnings before determining Section 125 CrPC maintenance quantum.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT allow husband to claim inflated, undocumented personal expenses to escape liability; deductions must be supported by authentic foreign documentation.
Calculator Dependency: Configurable overseas deduction engine.

Case Title: Baiju v. Hema
Judges: A. Muhamed Mustaque, C.S. Dias, JJ.
Acts Cited: Code of Criminal Procedure 1973, Indian Evidence Act 1872, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023
Sections Cited: Section 125 CrPC, Section 114(g) Evidence Act, Section 119(g) BSA, Section 106 Evidence Act, Section 109 BSA
Legal Topics: Concealment of Foreign Income, Adverse Inference, Burden of Proof, NRI Maintenance Quantum
Outcome: Appeal Disposed; Family Court's adverse inference against NRI husband upheld; maintenance awarded based on estimated foreign income.
Fact/Petitioner: Wife and minor child filed for maintenance under Section 125 CrPC in Family Court, claiming husband was working in UAE earning a substantial tax-free salary.
Fact/Respondent: Husband filed objections denying employment, claiming unemployment, and deliberately failed to produce his passport, visa, labor contract, or UAE bank statements.
Issues: Can the court draw an adverse inference under Section 114(g) Evidence Act (now Section 119(g) BSA) against an NRI spouse who suppresses foreign income, and what is the standard for imputing salary?
Petitioner Argument: Husband is gainfully employed abroad; all employment and financial documents are within his exclusive knowledge under Section 106 Evidence Act (now Section 109 BSA). Non-production warrants adverse inference.
Respondent Argument: Burden of proving husband's income lies on the petitioner; in absence of positive documentary proof, court cannot assume a high income.
Factors to be Considered: Section 106 Evidence Act / Section 109 BSA (fact especially within knowledge); Section 114(g) Evidence Act / Section 119(g) BSA (withholding evidence); qualification, professional skills, and overseas lifestyle.
Decision: Kerala High Court ruled that when an NRI husband withholds his foreign passport, employment visa, and salary records, the court must draw an adverse inference and assess maintenance on realistic estimated market income.
Exact Holding: True holding: Division Bench held that deliberate withholding of foreign employment proof by an NRI husband triggers adverse inference under Section 114(g) Evidence Act, entitling the court to estimate income based on qualification and lifestyle.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT allow the court to pluck arbitrary or astronomical figures out of thin air. The adverse inference must be grounded in realistic professional benchmarks and circumstantial evidence.
Calculator Dependency: Discretionary Adverse Inference engine with benchmark salary calibrations.

Case Title: Kulwinder Kumar v. Seema
Acts Cited: Code of Criminal Procedure 1973
Legal Topics: Interim Sustenance Floor, Able-Bodied Husband Rule, NRI Husband in Italy, Section 125 CrPC
Outcome: Revision Dismissed; Interim maintenance of Rs 10,000 per month awarded to wife upheld.
Fact/Petitioner: Husband working in Italy filed revision against Family Court order directing interim maintenance of Rs 10,000 per month, claiming irregular employment and financial distress abroad.
Fact/Respondent: Wife residing in Punjab with no independent source of income sought basic interim maintenance to survive during trial.
Issues: Can an able-bodied NRI husband working in a developed European nation avoid paying interim maintenance by pleading lack of fixed employment or financial hardship abroad?
Petitioner Argument: Petitioner works on irregular contract wages in Italy and has high local survival expenditures; interim order of Rs 10,000 per month is excessive.
Respondent Argument: An able-bodied husband residing in Europe cannot abandon his wife in India without basic interim sustenance.
Factors to be Considered: Doctrine of able-bodied person; presumption that healthy individual can earn sufficient livelihood; interim maintenance is meant to prevent vagrancy and starvation; minimal cost of living in Punjab.
Decision: High Court held that an able-bodied husband living and working abroad cannot escape his liability to pay interim maintenance to his destitute wife in India.
Exact Holding: True holding: High Court held that an able-bodied NRI husband working in Italy cannot plead unemployment or financial strain to deny basic sustenance maintenance to his wife in India.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT establish a binding nationwide statutory floor of Rs. 20,000-35,000. Maintenance is always case-specific, determined by the facts, social standing, and actual financial capacity of the parties.
Calculator Dependency: Interim Sustenance Floor scenario (labeled as optional illustrative scenario, not a mandatory statutory floor).

Case Title: Suresh Nanda v. Central Bureau of Investigation
Acts Cited: Code of Criminal Procedure 1973, Passports Act 1967
Sections Cited: Section 104 CrPC, Section 102 CrPC, Section 10(3)(h) Passports Act
Legal Topics: Passport Impoundment, Police & Judicial Powers, Section 10(3)(h) Passports Act, CrPC Section 104 Limits
Outcome: Appeal Allowed; High Court order set aside; passport directed to be returned; Clarified that courts and police cannot impound passports directly.
Fact/Petitioner: Petitioner's passport was seized by CBI during search and retained indefinitely. Trial court and High Court declined to release passport, citing Section 104 CrPC.
Fact/Respondent: Investigating agency argued that Section 104 CrPC gives courts wide power to impound any document produced before it, including a passport.
Issues: Whether a court or police officer has the power under Section 104 CrPC to impound a passport, or whether impoundment is governed exclusively by Section 10(3) of the Passports Act 1967?
Petitioner Argument: Passports Act 1967 is a special Act dealing specifically with passports and overrides general provisions of Section 104 CrPC (generalia specialibus non derogant). Impounding power vests solely with the Passport Authority.
Respondent Argument: CrPC Section 104 empowers courts to impound any document to ensure accused's presence at trial.
Factors to be Considered: Distinction between temporary seizure (Section 102 CrPC) and permanent impounding (Section 10(3) Passports Act); maxim generalia specialibus non derogant; Article 21 fundamental right to travel abroad (Maneka Gandhi).
Decision: Supreme Court held that courts and police do NOT have statutory power to impound passports under Section 104 CrPC. Impounding can only be done by the Passport Authority under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act 1967.
Exact Holding: True holding: Supreme Court ruled that while police can seize a passport under Section 102 CrPC, neither the police nor the criminal court has the power to impound a passport under Section 104 CrPC. Impounding is the exclusive prerogative of the Passport Authority under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act 1967.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT prevent criminal courts or Family Courts from directing the Passport Authority to initiate impoundment proceedings under Section 10(3)(h) where summons or warrants have been issued against an absconding NRI spouse.
Calculator Dependency: Cross-border coercive remedies & Passports Act Section 10(3)(h) guidance.

Case Title: Neeraja Saraph v. Jayant V. Saraph & Anr.
Acts Cited: Constitution of India 1950, Hindu Marriage Act 1955
Legal Topics: NRI Desertion, Feasibility of Central Legislation, Protection of Women Married to NRIs, Permanent Alimony Award
Outcome: Appeal Allowed; High Court judgment reversed; Husband and father-in-law directed to pay Rs. 3,00,000 to deserted wife; Recommendations made for national legislation.
Fact/Petitioner: Petitioner, a teacher in Pune, married respondent who was settled in USA as a doctorate computer scientist. Shortly after marriage, husband returned to USA, fraudulently canceled wife's visa sponsorship, filed for foreign annulment, and deserted her penniless in India.
Fact/Respondent: Husband claimed marriage was void under US law and that Indian courts could not execute maintenance or damages against his overseas assets.
Issues: What legal safeguards must be evolved to protect Indian women married to NRIs against transnational desertion, and can Indian courts award capitalized maintenance against family properties?
Petitioner Argument: NRI husband entered into marriage deceitfully, enjoyed matrimonial relations, and abandoned the wife in India without resources, destroying her social standing.
Respondent Argument: Husband has acquired foreign domicile and obtained a decree abroad; Indian courts lack territorial jurisdiction over foreign earnings.
Factors to be Considered: Acute social problem of abandoned brides of NRIs; necessity of legislation safeguarding marriage; power of Supreme Court under Article 142 to do complete justice; liability of husband's domestic assets.
Decision: Supreme Court awarded Rs. 3 lakhs as permanent damages/maintenance and urged Parliament to enact legislation providing: (1) No marriage with NRI solemnized without passport/property details; (2) Adequate alimony assessed on foreign salary.
Exact Holding: True holding: Supreme Court recognized the rampant social menace of NRI husbands deserting Indian brides, awarded permanent maintenance under Article 142 against husband and his father, and formulated landmark guidelines for NRI marriage legislation.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT constitute a self-executing statutory code; recommendations prompted subsequent administrative safeguards (like compulsory registration and passport impoundment).
Calculator Dependency: Capitalized lump-sum permanent alimony estimation & overseas asset liability.

Case Title: Ruchi Majoo v. Sanjeev Majoo
Acts Cited: Guardians and Wards Act 1890, Code of Civil Procedure 1908
Legal Topics: Inter-Country Child Custody, Parens Patriae Jurisdiction, Foreign Court Custody Orders, Welfare of Minor
Outcome: Appeal Allowed; High Court order quashing custody petition set aside; Indian Family Court held to have jurisdiction to determine child custody despite foreign court order.
Fact/Petitioner: Mother brought minor son from California, USA to New Delhi, India due to marital discord and filed for custody under Section 9 Guardians and Wards Act in Delhi. Superior Court of California had passed a custody order directing return of child to USA.
Fact/Respondent: Father argued that the California court was the court of ordinary residence of the child, and Indian courts must enforce the foreign order under principles of international comity.
Issues: Whether Indian courts are bound by foreign custody decrees, or whether the Indian court has independent parens patriae jurisdiction to determine custody based on the child's welfare?
Petitioner Argument: Child is ordinary resident of Delhi where he is enrolled in school; paramount consideration is child's welfare, not blind comity to foreign courts.
Respondent Argument: Mother removed the child in breach of foreign jurisdiction; comity of courts requires summary repatriation to USA.
Factors to be Considered: Paramountcy of child's welfare over foreign orders; non-signatory status of India to 1980 Hague Convention; parens patriae jurisdiction of Indian courts; child's educational integration in India.
Decision: Supreme Court held that Indian courts are not bound blindly by foreign custody orders. The paramount consideration is always the welfare of the child, which Indian courts will determine independently.
Exact Holding: True holding: Supreme Court held that custody orders are never final and are always subject to child's welfare; foreign custody orders do not oust the parens patriae jurisdiction of Indian courts under Section 9 GWA.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT sanction parental child abduction; courts may order summary return if the child has not developed roots in India and repatriation is in the child's best interest.
Calculator Dependency: Child custody jurisdiction and child support evaluation.

Case Title: Nithya Anand Raghavan v. State (NCT of Delhi) & Anr.
Judges: Dipak Misra, A.M. Khanwilkar, Mohan M. Shantanagoudar, JJ.
Acts Cited: Guardians and Wards Act 1890, Constitution of India 1950
Legal Topics: Hague Abduction Convention Non-Signatory, Habeas Corpus Child Custody, Welfare of Child Over Foreign Comity
Outcome: Appeal Allowed; High Court order directing mother to take child back to UK set aside; Custody restored to mother in India.
Fact/Petitioner: Mother brought minor daughter to India from UK alleging domestic violence and physical assault by husband. Father secured wardship and return orders from High Court of Justice in London, and filed Habeas Corpus in Delhi High Court.
Fact/Respondent: Father argued that child was a British citizen ordinary resident in UK, and English court orders must be respected.
Issues: In a Habeas Corpus petition seeking return of a child brought to India from a foreign country, whether Indian courts should order summary return based on foreign court orders?
Petitioner Argument: India has consciously not signed the 1980 Hague Convention. Comity of courts must yield to the best interests and welfare of the child and protection of the mother from overseas abuse.
Respondent Argument: Child was wrongfully retained in India; foreign court is the most competent forum to decide custody.
Factors to be Considered: Status of India as non-signatory to Hague Convention; paramount welfare test; risk of psychological and physical harm to child upon forced return.
Decision: 3-Judge Bench held that Indian courts will not order summary return of child to foreign jurisdiction unless proven that return will not cause any psychological or physical harm to child.
Exact Holding: True holding: 3-judge bench affirmed that India's non-accession to Hague Abduction Convention means Indian courts will conduct independent welfare inquiries rather than summarily repatriating children to foreign jurisdictions.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT grant a blanket license for wrongful retention; if child is removed in violation of orders and has no roots in India, summary return can still be directed.
Calculator Dependency: Cross-border child support & international custody guidelines.

Case Title: Jasmeet Kaur v. Navtej Singh
Judges: Kurian Joseph, Mohan M. Shantanagoudar, JJ.
Acts Cited: Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Hindu Marriage Act 1955
Sections Cited: Section 41 Specific Relief Act, Section 13 CPC
Legal Topics: Anti-Suit Injunction, Foreign Divorce Restraint, Jurisdiction Over Transnational Marriages
Outcome: Appeal Allowed; Anti-suit injunction granted restraining husband from pursuing divorce in Connecticut, USA.
Fact/Petitioner: Parties married in Delhi under Hindu rites and later moved to USA. Differences arose, and wife returned to India with children. Husband instituted divorce proceedings in the Superior Court of Judicial District of Stamford, Connecticut, USA.
Fact/Respondent: Husband argued that both parties had resided in Connecticut, children were attending school there, and US court had legitimate personal jurisdiction.
Issues: Under what circumstances will an Indian court issue an anti-suit injunction to restrain an NRI spouse from pursuing divorce proceedings in a foreign court?
Petitioner Argument: Marriage was solemnized in India under Hindu Marriage Act. Wife has no financial means or visa status to effectively contest divorce in Connecticut. Foreign proceedings are vexatious and oppressive.
Respondent Argument: Foreign court is natural forum as cause of action arose there; Indian court cannot restrain a person from approaching a competent foreign court.
Factors to be Considered: Tests for anti-suit injunction: (1) Respondent amenable to personal jurisdiction of Indian court; (2) Injustice would result if foreign suit proceeds; (3) Foreign proceedings are oppressive or vexatious; (4) Balance of convenience.
Decision: Supreme Court granted anti-suit injunction, holding that forcing the wife to litigate in the USA without financial support or independent legal status is oppressive and vexatious.
Exact Holding: True holding: Supreme Court granted anti-suit injunction restraining NRI husband from prosecuting US divorce proceedings, holding that forcing an Indian wife without resources to defend herself in a foreign forum is oppressive and vexatious.
Negative Limitations: Anti-suit injunctions are granted sparingly and with great caution; cannot be granted where both parties are genuine permanent foreign residents or where foreign proceedings are already at an advanced stage with voluntary participation.
Calculator Dependency: Anti-suit injunction strategy against parallel foreign matrimonial proceedings.

Case Title: Harmeeta Singh v. Rajat Taneja
Acts Cited: Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Hindu Marriage Act 1955
Legal Topics: Anti-Suit Injunction, Restraint on US Divorce, Interim Maintenance in Civil Suit, Transnational Desertion
Outcome: Application Allowed; Husband restrained from proceeding with divorce in Indiana, USA; Husband directed to pay maintenance.
Fact/Petitioner: Parties married in New Delhi in 2002. Husband took wife to Indiana, USA, and abandoned her at the airport when she returned to India to attend a family emergency. Husband then filed for divorce in Hamilton County, Indiana.
Fact/Respondent: Husband refused to provide living expenses or airfare for wife to return to Indiana to contest the proceedings, claiming US court had jurisdiction.
Issues: Can an Indian court restrain an NRI husband from pursuing a foreign divorce action and grant maintenance in an independent civil suit for declaration?
Petitioner Argument: Husband married under Hindu rites and cannot abandon his wife and unilaterally procure an ex-parte dissolution abroad where she cannot afford to appear.
Respondent Argument: Indian courts lack extraterritorial jurisdiction to injunct a US state court proceeding.
Factors to be Considered: Principle in Satya v. Teja Singh; balance of convenience; oppressive nature of ex-parte foreign proceedings against an abandoned bride without means.
Decision: Delhi High Court restrained the husband from proceeding with the Indiana divorce and held that an Indian spouse without visa or financial support cannot be subjected to foreign litigation.
Exact Holding: True holding: Delhi High Court granted an interim anti-suit injunction against an Indiana divorce petition and held that leaving a wife stranded in India while pursuing divorce abroad constitutes vexatious and oppressive conduct.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT permanently extinguish foreign courts' powers; applies strictly as an in personam restraint against the litigant before Indian courts.
Calculator Dependency: Anti-suit injunction and overseas litigation maintenance expenses.

Case Title: Aditi alias Mithi v. Jitesh Sharma
Acts Cited: Code of Criminal Procedure 1973
Legal Topics: Affidavit of Assets and Liabilities, Strict Compliance with Rajnesh v. Neha, Child Maintenance
Outcome: Appeal Allowed; High Court order reducing maintenance set aside; Mandatory affidavit filing strictly reinforced.
Fact/Petitioner: Minor daughter through mother sought enhancement of maintenance against father who was gainfully employed in corporate sector.
Fact/Respondent: Father failed to file complete disclosure affidavit and claimed business losses.
Issues: Whether trial courts can determine or alter maintenance under Section 125 CrPC without insisting on strict compliance with the Rajnesh v. Neha disclosure affidavit?
Petitioner Argument: High Court drastically reduced child maintenance without any evidence or sworn affidavit from respondent disclosing real assets.
Respondent Argument: Financial condition deteriorated; maintenance should be based on oral evidence.
Factors to be Considered: Strict enforcement of Rajnesh v. Neha guidelines; necessity of sworn declaration of assets; best interest and educational expenditure of minor child.
Decision: Supreme Court held that filing of the Affidavit of Assets and Liabilities is mandatory in all maintenance proceedings; failure to file warrants adverse inference and strike off of defense.
Exact Holding: True holding: Supreme Court reiterated that filing of comprehensive affidavit of assets and liabilities as mandated in Rajnesh v. Neha is non-negotiable in all maintenance cases, including Section 125 CrPC proceedings.
Negative Limitations: Does NOT dispense with evidentiary inquiry where affidavits are contested; serves as baseline disclosure.
Calculator Dependency: Disclosure compliance and adverse inference triggers.

Case Title: Kusum Sharma v. Mahinder Kumar Sharma (I to V)
Acts Cited: Hindu Marriage Act 1955, Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Code of Criminal Procedure 1973
Sections Cited: Section 24 HMA, Section 125 CrPC, Section 10(3)(h) Passports Act
Legal Topics: Standardized Income Affidavits, NRI Disclosure Formats, Perjury for False Affidavits, Foreign Assets Tracking
Outcome: Landmark directions issued; Standardized affidavit formats (Format A to E) prescribed for all matrimonial maintenance proceedings across Delhi.
Fact/Petitioner: Wife in long-drawn matrimonial battle spanning over two decades sought realistic maintenance against wealthy husband who repeatedly concealed assets.
